post.html:
Imagine that you reverse engineered a piece of malware in pain-staking detail, only to find that the malware author created a slightly modified version of the malware the next day. You wouldn't want to redo all your hard work. One way to avoid this is to use code comparison techniques to try to identify pairs of functions in the old and new version that are "the same" (which I put in quotes because it's a bit of a nebulous concept as we'll see).

There are several tools to help in such situations. A very popular (formally) commercial tool is zynamics' bindiff, which is now owned by Google and free. CMU SEI's Pharos also includes a code comparison utility called fn2hash, which is the subject of this blog post.

Exact Hashing

fn2hash employs several types of hashing, with the most commonly used one called PIC hashing, where PIC stands for Position Independent Code. At a high level, the goal of PIC hashing is to compute a hash or signature of code, but do so in a way that relocating the code will not change the hash. This is important because modifying a program often results in small changes to addresses and offsets (and we don't want these changes to modify the hash!). PIC hashing starts off with the byte-by-byte code representation of a function. It disassembles the code, and uses the disassembly to identify any parts of the code that are addresses or offsets, and then zeros out the corresponding bytes. Finally, it applies a cryptographic hash function (e.g., md5) to create the hash.

Let's look at an example. I compiled this simple program with g++. Here's the beginning of the assembly code for the function myfunc (full code):

Assembly code and bytes from oo.gcc 
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;;; function 0x00401200 "myfunc()"
;;; mangled name is "_Z6myfuncv"
;;; reasons for function: referenced by symbol table

;; predecessor:  from instruction 0x004010f4 from basic block 0x004010f0
0x00401200: 41 56                      00 push     r140x00401202: bf 60 00 00 00            -08 mov      edi, 0x00000060<96>
0x00401207: 41 55                     -08 push     r13
0x00401209: 41 54                     -10 push     r12
0x0040120b: 55                        -18 push     rbp
0x0040120c: 48 83 ec 08               -20 sub      rsp, 8
0x00401210: e8 bb fe ff ff            -28 call     function 0x004010d0 "operator new(unsigned long)@plt"

Exact bytes

In this listing, you can see that the first instruction is a push r14, which is encoded by the bytes 41 56. If we collect the full bytes for the function, we get

Exact bytes in oo.gcc 


We call this sequence the exact bytes of the function. We can hash these bytes to get an exact hash, 62CE2E852A685A8971AF291244A1283A.

Motivation for PIC Hashing

If you look at the call at address 0x00401210, it includes the bytes bb fe ff ff, which is 0xfffffebb in little endian form. As a signed value, this is -325. If we take the address of the next instruction (0x401210 + 5 == 0x401215) and then add -325 to it, we get 0x4010d0, which is the address of operator new, the target of the call. Yay. So now we know that bb fe ff ff is an offset from the next instruction.

I created a slightly modified program (oo2.gcc) by adding an empty, unused function before myfunc. You can find the disassembly of myfunc for this executable here.

If we take the exact hash of this function, we get 05718F65D9AA5176682C6C2D5404CA8D. Wait, that's different than the hash in the other executable, 62CE2E852A685A8971AF291244A1283A. What happened? Let's look at the disassembly.

Assembly code and bytes from oo2.gcc 
;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;;
;;; function 0x00401210 "myfunc()"

;; predecessor:  from instruction 0x004010f4 from basic block 0x004010f0
0x00401210: 41 56                      00 push     r140x00401212: bf 60 00 00 00            -08 mov      edi, 0x00000060<96>
0x00401217: 41 55                     -08 push     r13
0x00401219: 41 54                     -10 push     r12
0x0040121b: 55                        -18 push     rbp
0x0040121c: 48 83 ec 08               -20 sub      rsp, 8
0x00401220: e8 ab fe ff ff            -28 call     function 0x004010d0 "operator new(unsigned long)@plt"

Notice that myfunc moved from 0x401200 to 0x401210, which also moved the address of the call instruction from 0x401210 to 0x401220. Because the call target is specified as an offset from the (next) instruction's address, which changed by 0x10 == 16, the offset bytes for the call changed from bb fe ff ff (-325) to ab fe ff ff (-341 == -325 - 16). These changes modify the exact bytes to:

Exact bytes in oo2.gcc 


You can look through that and see the differences by eyeballing it. Just kidding! Here's a visual comparison. Red represents bytes that are only in oo.gcc, and green represents bytes in oo2.gcc. The differences are small because the offset is only changing by 0x10, but it's enough to break exact hashing.

Difference between exact bytes in oo.gcc and oo2.gcc 


PIC Hashing

This problem is the motivation for few different types of hashing that we'll talk about in this blog post, including PIC hashing and fuzzy hashing. The PIC in PIC hashing stands for Position Independent Code. The idea of PIC hashing is really simple: identify offsets and addresses that are likely to change if the program is recompiled, such as bb fe ff ff, and simply set them to zero before hashing the bytes. That way if they change, it won't change the function's hash.

If we do this on our example function, we obtain the following PIC bytes:

PIC bytes from oo.gcc (which are the same as oo2.gcc) 


Here's another visual diff between the exact bytes and the PIC bytes. Red represents bytes that are only in the PIC bytes, and green represents bytes in the exact bytes. As expected, the first change we can see is the byte sequence bb fe ff ff, which is changed to zeros.

Byte difference 


If we hash the PIC bytes, we get the PIC hash EA4256ECB85EDCF3F1515EACFA734E17. And, as we would expect, we get the same PIC hash for the slightly modified oo2.gcc.

Evaluating the Accuracy of PIC Hashing

There are some downsides to PIC Hashing. What if two pieces of code are compiled with different compilers or different compiler flags? What if two pieces of code are very similar, but one had a line of code removed? Because these changes would modify the non-offset bytes that are used in the PIC hash, I would expect them to change the hash of the code. PIC hashing would consider all of these changes to create a different version of the code.

So how can we define the accuracy of PIC hashing (or similar techniques)? Well, one common trick is to use compiler debug symbols to map function addresses to names. For each executable, this gives us a ground truth set of functions and their names. For the purposes of this blog post, we'll assume that if two functions have the same name, they are "the same". (This obviously is not true in general!)

So, let's say we have two similar executables, and we want to evaluate how well PIC hashing can identify similar functions across both functions. We'll start by considering all possible pairs of functions, where each pair has one function from each executable. If we're being mathy, this is called the cartesian product. For each pair, we'll use the ground truth to determine if the functions are the same, by seeing if they have the same name. Then we'll use PIC hashing to predict whether the functions are the same by computing their hashes and seeing if they are identical.

Confusion Matrices

Consider a pair of functions. We can separate each result in two dimensions. First, whether the ground truth says the functions are equivalent. And second, whether PIC hashing predicts they are equivalent. We can give a name to each possibility:

  • True Positive: PIC hashing correctly predicted the functions are equivalent.
  • True Negative: PIC hashing correctly predicted the functions are different.
  • False Positive: PIC hashing incorrectly predicted the functions are equivalent, but they are not.
  • False Negative: PIC hashing incorrectly predicted the functions are different, but they are equivalent.

We can represent these in what is called a confusion matrix:

Hashing says same Hashing says different
Ground truth says same TP FN
Ground truth says different FP TN

For example, here is a confusion matrix comparing the functions in oo.gcc (oo.cpp compiled with gcc) and oo.clang (oo.cpp compiled with clang) using PIC hashing:

Hashing says same Hashing says different
Ground truth says same 4 9
Ground truth says different 2 308

We can use these to compute a few different metrics. Accuracy is probably the most natural one: How many pairs did hashing predict correctly? This is equal to (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FN + FT). For the above example, hashing achieved an accuracy of (4 + 308) / (4 + 308 + 9 + 2) = 0.966. 96.6% accuracy, not bad, right?

But if you look closely, there's a subtle problem. Most pairs of functions are not equivalent. According to the ground truth, there are TP + FN = 4 + 9 = 13 equivalent function pairs, and TN + FP = 308 + 2 = 310 non-equivalent function pairs. So, if we just guessed that all pairs of functions were non-equivalent, we would be right 310 / (310 + 13) = 96.0% of the time. So, accuracy might not be the best metric here.

Two other metrics that focus more on positive cases (i.e., equivalent functions) are precision and recall:

  • Recall: Of the equivalent function pairs, how many did hashing correctly identify? This is equal to TP / (TP + FN).
  • Precision: Of the function pairs hashing identified as equivalent, how many were actually equivalent? This is equal to TP / (TP + FP).

Intuitively, recall will tell us how many equivalent function pairs hashing is correctly predicting, and precision reveals how many of the function pairs it predicts as equivalent are actually equivalent. These metrics both focus on the positive results, which in this case corresponds to equivalent pairs of functions. This is consistent with reverse engineering, because the reverse engineer is usually interesting in pairs that are equivalent between two binaries, because this allows them to transfer knowledge from one executable to another.

For the above example, hashing achieved a recall of 4 / (4 + 9) = 0.308, and a precision of 4 / (4 + 2) = 0.667. So, hashing is only able to identify 30.8% of equivalent function pairs, but when it does predict a pair is equivalent, it is correct 66.7% of the time. Imagine that you spent hours reverse engineering the 13 functions in one of the executables, only to find that PIC hashing was only able to identify 4 of them in the other executable, so you would be forced to needlessly reverse engineer the other 9 functions from scratch. That would be pretty frustrating! Can we do better?
